claims.text: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a room-temperature yield strength of approximately 1600 MPa.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has an elevated-temperature yield strength of approximately 855 MPa.
Partially replacing Hf with lighter Al will reduce the density of HfMoTaTiZr.
Limited Al substitution will maintain the room- and elevated-temperature yield strengths of HfMoTaTiZr.
Controlled Al addition can provide solid-solution strengthening in the BCC matrix.
Controlled Al addition will not disrupt the beneficial dislocation-slip mechanisms of HfMoTaTiZr.
Arc melting Al0.1–0.15Hf0.9–0.85MoTaTiZr will produce a homogeneous, single-phase BCC alloy.
The Al-modified alloy will preserve the BCC structure and its associated lattice distortion.
Preserving the BCC structure and lattice distortion will sustain yield strength and dislocation mobility.
Al introduces additional lattice distortion that can enhance solid-solution strengthening.
Maintaining the BCC structure preserves an effective transition between screw- and edge-dislocation-controlled plasticity at room and high temperatures.
The modified alloy will have a density approximately 10–15% below the as-cast baseline.
The modified alloy will retain a room-temperature yield strength near 1600 MPa.
The modified alloy will retain a yield strength near 850 MPa at 1000 °C.
Excessive Al could destabilize the phase or degrade ductility.
Mechanical performance will be evaluated at 298 K and 1000 °C at a strain rate of approximately 1×10⁻³ s⁻¹.
A 0%, 5%, 10%, and 15% Hf-to-Al substitution series made under identical processing conditions will isolate the effect of Al.
The hypothesis is rejected unless an Al-containing alloy has density below approximately 9.5 g/cm³ and retains at least 90% of baseline yield strength at both 298 K and 1000 °C.

contradictions.description: A predicted 10–15% reduction from 10.21 g/cm³ corresponds to approximately 8.68–9.19 g/cm³, whereas the rejection criterion accepts any density below 9.5 g/cm³, only about a 7% reduction. Thus, the falsification threshold does not test the stated quantitative prediction.
The hypothesis says strength will be maintained without sacrifice, while the rejection rule permits yield strengths to fall to 90% of baseline at both temperatures.

The boundary suggests tensile or compressive behavior is to be assessed at both temperatures, but the specified experiment uses tensile loading at 298 K and compression at 1000 °C. This confounds temperature with loading mode and prevents direct like-for-like strength retention across temperatures.
